extracted.subtask_description: Solving and constructing solutions to Euclidean geometry problems (regular polygons, transformations, constructions, and physically flavored geometry) using classical synthetic, trigonometric, complex-number, and transformation-based methods. Emphasizes heuristics, constructions with straightedge/compass, and contest-style reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden rotation / 60°-rotation heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Recall that if we rotate a point B around a point A by 60° to a point C, the triangle ABC is equilateral. This implies that an isosceles triangle with an angle of 60° is equilateral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 60° rotations to reveal equilateral triangles or to obtain that two lines are images of each other under a 60° rotation (e.g., obtain that BM is the 60°-rotation of CN, so the lines form a 60° angle). Look for a hidden rotation as a way to simplify equilateral-triangle problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use similar triangles to relate segments after rotation/parallel constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: From similar triangles MQA and MBC deduce AQ/BC = MA/MC = MA/(MA + BC); from similar triangles NMA and NDB deduce NA/NB = MA/BD. With AB = BC = BD it follows that NA/AB = MA/(MA + BC) = AQ/AB, hence AQ = NA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a rotation/parallel leads to triangles that appear similar, set up the similarity ratios to deduce equal lengths and conclude equilateral or symmetric properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Pascal (projective) for degenerate cyclic hexagons
rubrics_metrics.description: When tangents and chords form a degenerate cyclic hexagon ABBRCC, by Pascal’s theorem the pairs of opposite sides intersect at collinear points. This can show that intersections lie on the circumcircle or coincide with constructed points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Pascal to degenerate hexagons composed of tangents and sides to deduce collinearity and to identify intersection points on circles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotate by 45° + homothety for square center construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The center of a square can be obtained by rotating one of the vertices about an adjacent vertex by 45° and then contracting with respect to the center of rotation by a ratio of 1/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model rotations and contractions using complex numbers to express these operations algebraically when constructing centers of squares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use complex numbers (trigonometric form) for polygon symmetry and rotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiplication by e^{iα} yields a counterclockwise rotation of angle α. Place figures in complex plane (origin at center) to derive coordinates of rotated points and midpoints leading to regularity conclusions (e.g., show midpoints Ci form a regular hexagon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express vertex coordinates as complex numbers and use multiplication by roots of unity to represent rotations; compare coordinates to show regularity and symmetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometric side/arc relations for regular n-gons
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscribe a heptagon in a circle of radius R: AB = 2R sin(π/7), AC = 2R sin(2π/7), AD = 2R sin(3π/7). Translate required algebraic identities into trigonometric identities (e.g., 1/sin(π/7) = 1/sin(2π/7) + 1/sin(3π/7)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert geometric equalities into sine/cosine relations using chord = 2R sin(angle/2) or equivalent; then use product-to-sum or sum-to-product formulas and known cosine symmetries (cos(π − x) = −cos x) to prove identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ptolemy's theorem as tool in regular polygon problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Ptolemy’s theorem to cyclic quadrilaterals appearing inside regular polygons to derive algebraic relations among side lengths (e.g., ab + ac = bc leading to a/b + a/c = 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify cyclic quadrilaterals in the figure and write Ptolemy relations to translate geometric constraints into algebraic equalities; these often yield useful telescoping or ratio identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use roots of unity and polynomial arguments for global regularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Place polygon vertices as Rε^i where ε are nth roots of unity. Consider products ∏|x − ε_i| and use the identity ∏(x − εi) = x^n − 1 to prove equalities like ∏PAi = POn − Rn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model coordinates by roots of unity and leverage algebraic factorization (cyclotomic polynomials) and polynomial uniqueness to deduce that a given configuration must be regular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescoping trigonometric sums via doubling/multiplication tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: Scale (e.g., set α = π/(2n+1)) and multiply desired identity by 2 cos(α/2) so that 2 cos kα cos(α/2) becomes a sum of cosines that telescopes; thereby derive sum identities like ∑(−1)^{k−1} cos(kπ/(2n+1)) = 1/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn sums into forms amenable to telescoping by multiplying with a suitable cosine factor and using sum-to-product/product-to-sum to cancel terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area and AM–HM inequalities for regular n-gon bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Area of regular n-gon of side a equals (n a^2)/(4 tan(π/n)). Use tan x > x and arithmetic–harmonic mean inequality to bound sums and reciprocals of triangle areas formed with a point M inside polygon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate area formulas to sums of triangle areas to obtain inequalities; apply standard calculus/trig inequalities (tan x > x) and mean inequalities to obtain numeric bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive use of complex coordinates for explicit vertex identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign convenient complex coordinates (e.g., 2a,2b,2c,2d) to avoid fractions, compute images under rotations/dilations explicitly, and deduce orthogonality or rotation relations between segments (e.g., q − n = i(p − m) so NQ is a 90°-rotation of MP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose scalings that simplify algebra; compute coordinates of constructed points and compare differences to detect rotations by multiplication by i or e^{iπ/2}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: solve 'backwards' using uniqueness/symmetry to construct desired point
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a triangle MCD is equilateral inside a regular pentagon, construct the unique point M' such that M'CD is equilateral, then use symmetry/angle computations to show that M = M'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When uniqueness of a symmetric construction is available, build the candidate configuration and verify it satisfies the given constraints rather than attempting to derive it forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting edges/angles combinatorial argument in triangle dissections
rubrics_metrics.description: Count edges and angles (with multiplicity) in dissections to bound the number of vertices/angles on sides/interior; use parity and repetition counts to derive contradictions (e.g., at most one vertex on sides of triangle BMC or at least 13 sides impossibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combinatorial counting (edges counted per incident triangle, angles per vertex) to show impossibility of certain dissections; account for double-counting and triangle side counts carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit angle-chasing constraints to force specific angle measures
rubrics_metrics.description: If three triangles meet at an interior vertex and all their angles equal γ, then γ = 120°, leading to contradictions or concrete angle assignments; use relations like γ = α + β when triangle is not right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine angle-sum relations and local meeting conditions (how many triangles at a vertex) to deduce specific angle measures; check for consistency with global triangle angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct center of a circle using compass-only inversion and reflections
rubrics_metrics.description: With only a compass one can invert a point with respect to a known circle, reflect a point across a line given two points on that line, and use that the image of the center O under inversion is the reflection of the inversion center Q across the line AB (where AB is image of circle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find the center: pick Q on the circle, draw a larger circle centered at Q intersecting original circle at A,B; reflect Q across AB to get O' (image of O); invert O' with respect to circle centered at Q to recover O. Use the described constructions for inversion and reflection using compass-only steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct reflection across a line using two points on the line (compass only)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reflection of P with respect to line AB can be constructed as the second intersection of the circle of center A radius AP with the circle of center B radius BP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When only two points of the mirror line are given, use equal-radius circles centered at these two points to find the reflected point as the second intersection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct rotations by composing equilateral-triangle constructions and translations
rubrics_metrics.description: To rotate B around A by 60°, partition the segment AB into unit steps P0=A,...,Pn=B. Construct equilateral triangle P0P1Q1 to get Q1 = rotation of P1 about A; then translate/rotate inductively: translate Pk to Rk by vector P_{k−1}Q_{k−1} and rotate Rk about R_{k−1} by 60° to get Qk. Qn is the rotation of B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement rotations with straightedge/compass by building a chain of small equal steps and composing elementary equilateral-triangle rotations and translations; inductive construction yields exact rotation of the endpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct rotation+dilation (composition) using translations + rotation+dilation about successive points
rubrics_metrics.description: To effect a rotation followed by dilation about A (e.g., 90° and ratio √3/3), use the property that a rotation–dilation of center M can be obtained by translating P to P' by vector NN' and then rotating/dilating around N' (image of N). Implement inductively as in pure rotation construction but replacing the rotation step by rotation–dilation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simulate a rotation-dilation by local operations: translate along known vectors then perform rotation and dilation about newly obtained centers; build inductively over partition of segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate geometric transformation problems into vector/area identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Sum of vectors orthogonal to polygon sides (lengths equal to side lengths) is proportional to rotated closing vector; for polyhedra the sum of face-normal vectors weighted by face areas equals zero (equilibrium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with polygons/polyhedra, express conditions via vectors and areas: vector sums, projections, and volumes can give compact proofs (e.g., equilibrium interpretation of Pascal/forces, or additive area decompositions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physical intuition (equilibrium, shortest path / Fermat principle) as geometric heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret geometric problems physically: forces on faces (Pascal's law) imply equilibrium and vector sums zero; light path in dense medium follows quickest path so the bridge+river shortest-connection problem is solved by translating cities by width of river and taking straight line (Fermat principle analogy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate geometric optimization or balance problems into physical analogies (gravitational potential, light refraction) to guide rigorous geometric constructions and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centroid linearity property for combinatorial centroid constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Centroid of k+j points divides segment G1G2 (centroids of two groups) in ratio j:k. Use this to prove concurrency or common-point properties obtained from centroids and perpendiculars to chords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use centroid additivity and mass-point style reasoning to derive ratios and collinearity/concurrency properties when centroids of subsets are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use signed volumes and dot-product identities in tetrahedron proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Volume differences P_BCD(x) − P_BCD(y) equal (1/3)((y − x) · v4), and summing over faces yields constraints that imply vector sums of face-normal-area vectors vanish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use signed volumes and linearity to convert geometric face-area-vector statements into dot-product equalities that must hold for all test vectors, yielding vector-sum conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inequalities for tetrahedron dihedral-angle cosines via vector norm identity
rubrics_metrics.description: For unit outward normals v_i to faces, sum S of cosines of dihedral angles equals 2 − (1/2)(v1 + v2 + v3 + v4)^2, hence S ≤ 2 with equality iff face-areas equal (after proportionality argument).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express S through dot products of face-normal vectors; use square-of-sum identity and known vector-sum results to get numerical bounds and characterize equality cases.
